title: Best Sneakers to Buy in Kenya: A Practical Buyer's Guide
excerpt: Not sure where to start? Here's how to think about picking a sneaker in Kenya, whatever your budget or use case.
body:
Walk into any mall in Nairobi and you'll find dozens of sneaker options, which is part of the problem: too much choice with too little guidance. Here's a practical way to narrow it down, whether you're buying your first proper pair or adding to a growing collection.

Start with how you'll actually use them

A sneaker for the office is not the same as one for the gym or for a night out. If you're after something that goes with jeans, chinos and most smart-casual outfits, a clean white or neutral silhouette from Nike or Adidas is the safest bet. If comfort for long days on your feet matters more than looks, prioritise a cushioned sole and breathable upper over the flashiest colourway.

Decide on a brand direction, not just a shoe

Nike, Adidas, Jordan and Puma each have a distinct look. Nike tends to lean bold with statement colourways. Adidas leans retro and understated. Jordan sits somewhere in between, with heritage silhouettes that work as much for style as for sport. None of these is objectively "better" — it's about what suits your wardrobe and how often you'll actually wear it.

Sizing is where most buyers go wrong

Sneaker sizing varies by brand and sometimes by model. If you've never owned a particular brand before, don't assume your usual size will fit — check the specific size chart, and when in doubt, message the shop before you order. We're happy to confirm fit over WhatsApp for anyone unsure.

Budget realistically

You don't need to spend the most to get a good sneaker. A well-chosen budget pair in a versatile colourway will get more wear than an expensive pair that only matches two outfits. Set a budget range first, then shop within it rather than falling for the first eye-catching pair you see.

Buy from somewhere that stands behind what it sells

Authenticity matters more in Kenya's sneaker market than it should have to. Buy from a shop that's transparent about where its stock comes from and lets you inspect the shoe in person before paying, whether that's us or anyone else. It's the single best protection against ending up with a fake.

title: How to Style Air Force 1s: Outfit Ideas That Actually Work
excerpt: The Air Force 1 goes with almost everything — here's how to wear it well instead of just wearing it.
body:
The Air Force 1 has stayed a wardrobe staple for one simple reason: it's genuinely versatile. A clean silhouette and a mostly-neutral palette mean it slots into more outfits than almost any other sneaker. Here's how to get the most out of a pair.

The classic: jeans, a plain tee, white AF1s

This combination works because nothing competes for attention. Straight or slim-fit jeans, a well-fitted plain tee, and a clean white pair. It's the outfit that works everywhere from a casual Friday at the office to a weekend out.

Smart-casual: chinos and a button-down

Swap the jeans for chinos and the tee for a button-down shirt, and the same sneaker instantly reads more polished. This is the move for a date, a family event, or any setting that calls for slightly more effort without going full formal.

Black AF1s for a sharper look

A black pair reads more serious than white. Pair with dark denim or black trousers and a fitted jacket for an outfit that still feels relaxed but leans smarter.

Layering for cooler evenings

Nairobi evenings can get cool, especially in the rainy season. A hoodie or light jacket over a plain outfit keeps the sneakers as the focal point rather than competing with a busy top layer.

Keep them clean

Because AF1s are usually light-coloured, they show dirt fast. A pair that's scuffed or grubby undoes the whole outfit, however good the styling. See our guide on keeping white sneakers looking fresh for a simple cleaning routine.

title: Nike vs Adidas: Which Suits You Better in Kenya?
excerpt: Both brands are everywhere in Kenya's sneaker scene. Here's how they actually differ, beyond the logo.
body:
Nike or Adidas is one of the most common questions we get asked in the shop. There's no universally correct answer, but there are real differences worth knowing before you decide.

Style direction

Nike tends toward bold, sporty silhouettes — think Air Max and Air Force lines, with statement colourways and chunkier soles on some models. Adidas leans retro, with the Samba and Campus lines favouring a flatter, more understated profile that's found a second life in streetwear far beyond the football pitch.

Fit and comfort

Fit varies by specific model more than by brand overall, which is exactly why sizing guides matter — see our sneaker size guide before ordering either brand for the first time. As a general pattern, Adidas silhouettes like the Samba run a touch narrower than many Nike models, but this varies enough by shoe that it's worth checking specifics rather than assuming.

Versatility

Both brands offer genuinely versatile options. A white Air Force 1 and a white Samba both go with almost anything — the choice there really does come down to which silhouette you personally prefer.

What we'd suggest

If you want something bold that stands out, lean Nike. If you want something that quietly works with everything and has a retro edge, lean Adidas. Neither is the wrong answer — the best sneaker is the one you'll actually reach for every day.

title: How to Clean White Sneakers Without Ruining Them
excerpt: White sneakers look great for about a week. Here's how to keep them that way for a lot longer.
body:
White sneakers are one of the most versatile things you can own, and also the fastest to look tired. The good news is that keeping them clean doesn't require anything specialist — just a bit of consistency.

What you'll need

  • A soft-bristle brush (an old toothbrush works fine)
  • Mild soap or a dedicated sneaker cleaner
  • A microfibre cloth
  • Warm water
  • Shoe trees, if you have them, to help the shoe keep its shape while drying

Step by step

Start by removing the laces and insoles — wash the laces separately in soapy water so you're not scrubbing around them. Brush off any loose dirt while the shoe is still dry; wetting caked-on dirt first just turns it into paste that's harder to remove.

Mix a small amount of mild soap into warm water, dip the brush, and work in small circular motions over the upper. Focus on one section at a time rather than soaking the whole shoe at once — leather and canvas both handle a light, controlled clean far better than a full soak.

Wipe away the soap with a damp microfibre cloth, then a dry one to lift excess moisture. Stuff the shoe loosely with paper or use shoe trees to help it hold its shape, and let it air dry away from direct sun or a heater — direct heat can warp soles and crack certain materials.

What to avoid

Skip the washing machine. It's tempting, but the agitation and heat can separate glued soles and damage cushioning far faster than hand cleaning wears a shoe down. Also avoid bleach on anything with coloured detailing, even small logo accents — it can bleed and stain the surrounding white.

Maintenance beats restoration

A quick wipe-down after a dusty day is far easier than a deep clean after weeks of neglect. If you're regularly on Nairobi's roads and pavements, a five-minute wipe once or twice a week keeps white sneakers looking new for much longer.

title: Sneaker Size Guide: How to Get Your Fit Right the First Time
excerpt: Ordering online means you can't try before you buy — here's how to measure and choose correctly.
body:
Getting the size right matters more when you're ordering online than when you're trying shoes on in person. Here's a simple way to measure at home, plus a few notes on how sizing tends to vary between brands.

Measuring your foot

Stand on a piece of paper against a wall, with your heel touching the wall. Mark the tip of your longest toe, then measure the distance from the wall to that mark in centimetres. Do this for both feet in the evening, when feet are naturally slightly larger, and use the bigger measurement.

Why brand matters, not just size number

A UK 9 or EU 43 isn't always identical across brands. Nike and Adidas both publish their own size charts, and small differences in last shape (the mould a shoe is built around) mean the same labelled size can fit slightly differently. If you're trying a brand for the first time, it's worth checking that specific brand's chart rather than assuming your usual number carries over.

When you're between sizes

As a general rule, if you're between two sizes, sizing up is usually the safer choice for sneakers — a slightly loose fit is more comfortable over a full day than a slightly tight one, and you can always add a thicker insole or sock.

If you're still not sure

Message us on WhatsApp with the exact shoe you're considering and your usual size in any brand you already own — we can often tell you directly how it compares. It's a lot easier to check before ordering than to arrange an exchange after.

title: What's Actually Trending in Kenyan Streetwear Right Now
excerpt: From Westlands to Nyali, here's what's showing up most in Kenya's streetwear scene.
body:
Kenya's streetwear scene has grown fast, and it's developed its own identity rather than simply copying trends from elsewhere. Here's what we're actually seeing move in the shop and around Nairobi.

Custom and personalised sneakers

Custom colourways and hand-finished detailing on classic silhouettes are increasingly popular — buyers want something that isn't identical to what everyone else is wearing, even on a familiar shoe shape.

Retro is back, properly

Silhouettes from the 80s and 90s — think chunky retro runners and flat-soled court shoes — have found a genuinely new audience rather than just nostalgia buyers. They pair naturally with the current preference for looser, more relaxed fits in everything else.

Neutral palettes dominate

White, black, grey and beige are doing most of the heavy lifting in outfits right now. It's a practical trend as much as a stylistic one — neutral sneakers pair with almost any wardrobe, which matters when you're building a capsule of pieces that all work together.

Function alongside style

There's a growing preference for shoes that genuinely hold up to Nairobi's roads and weather, not just ones that look good in photos. Durable soles and materials that clean up easily are increasingly a deciding factor, not an afterthought.

Where this leaves you

You don't need to chase every trend. A couple of well-chosen neutral sneakers, one classic retro pair, and one statement piece will cover most of what's actually happening in Kenyan streetwear right now — without needing a wardrobe overhaul.

title: How to Spot Fake Sneakers: A Practical Buyer's Guide
excerpt: Counterfeit sneakers are a real risk in Kenya's market. Here's what to actually check before you buy.
body:
Counterfeit sneakers are common enough in Kenya that it's worth knowing what to check before handing over your money, wherever you're buying from.

Check the stitching

Genuine sneakers have clean, even stitching with consistent spacing. Fakes often show loose threads, uneven lines, or visible glue around the heel counter and toe box. Look closely at these areas rather than just the overall shape of the shoe.

Feel the materials

Real leather has a distinct texture and smell, and feels noticeably more premium than the stiff, plastic-like synthetic materials commonly used in counterfeits. If a "leather" shoe feels like it's made of thin plastic, that's a warning sign.

Examine the branding closely

Logos on genuine sneakers are precise — even spacing, correct proportions, consistent colour. Counterfeits frequently get small details wrong: a slightly off font, uneven logo placement, or stitching around a logo that doesn't quite match the rest of the shoe.

Weight and sole quality

Genuine sneakers usually feel more substantial and have a sole with clearly defined tread patterns and consistent colour. A sole that feels unusually light, thin, or has a blurry, poorly defined pattern is worth a second look.

Price that seems too good

If a price is dramatically lower than what the same shoe sells for elsewhere, treat that as a signal to investigate further rather than a lucky find. Genuine stock has a cost floor that a seller can't go below and still be selling the real thing.

The simplest protection

Buy somewhere you can inspect the shoe in person before paying, and that's transparent about where its stock comes from. That single habit removes most of the risk, regardless of which shop you choose.

title: 10 Sneaker Colourways That Never Go Out of Style
excerpt: Some colourways just work, year after year. Here's what to reach for if you want longevity over trend-chasing.
body:
Trends come and go, but certain sneaker colourways stay relevant regardless of what's currently popular. If you want a pair that'll still look right in a few years, these are the safest choices.

All-white

The single most versatile option there is. A clean white sneaker goes with almost any outfit, from smart-casual to sportswear, and works across every season.

Black and white

The classic contrast combination. It reads slightly sharper than pure white without losing any of the versatility, and hides scuffs a little better too.

All-black

A black sneaker is quietly one of the most useful things you can own. It dresses down a smart outfit or dresses up a casual one, and works well after dark in a way lighter colours don't.

Grey

Understated and easy to pair with almost anything, grey sits nicely between the boldness of black and the brightness of white — a genuinely underrated choice.

Navy

More sophisticated than most other colours without tipping into formal. Navy pairs particularly well with denim and khaki tones.

Why timeless beats trendy

A statement colourway is fun, but it dates and it limits what you can wear it with. A wardrobe built around two or three of the colours above, plus one bolder pair for when you want to stand out, will outlast almost any trend-driven purchase.

title: Why Buying New Shoes Is Worth It, Beyond Just Looking Good
excerpt: New shoes do more for you than update your look — here's what actually changes when you retire a worn-out pair.
body:
It's easy to keep wearing a pair long after they've served their purpose, but there are real, practical reasons to replace worn-out shoes rather than just an aesthetic one.

Comfort and support

Cushioning breaks down with use, even when a shoe still looks fine on the outside. Worn-out support can mean more foot fatigue by the end of the day, something that's easy not to notice until you compare it to a fresh pair.

Confidence, plainly

There's a genuine, if less measurable, boost that comes from wearing something that looks and feels new. It's not vanity — feeling put-together affects how you carry yourself through the day.

Better for your feet long-term

Shoes that have lost their structure can change how you walk without you noticing, which over time can contribute to discomfort elsewhere — ankles, knees, even your back. Replacing shoes before they're fully worn out is a small habit with a real payoff.

A practical reset

A new pair is also a natural point to reconsider what you actually need in your rotation — maybe it's time for a more versatile colour, or a style that better suits how your week actually looks now compared to when you bought the last pair.

When to actually replace a pair

Visible sole wear, a upper that's stretched out of shape, or cushioning that's noticeably flatter than when new are all good signals it's time. You don't need to wait until a shoe is falling apart to justify a new one.
